ICYMI, last week I compared @worldnetwork and @Concordium’s different approaches to private identity.

This week I went through some of their docs, and I found a few more things that make those differences a bit clearer when it comes to AI agents.

World starts with proof of personhood. A verified human can delegate their World ID to an agent, proving that a real, unique human sits behind it. That’s especially useful for Sybil resistance.

Concordium $CCD approaches the problem differently:

Its Agent Registry gives the agent its own onchain identity anchor, linked to the verified human or business behind it. Each agent can also carry a declared scope of what it's authorised to do, recorded onchain.

That’s an essential distinction.

Once agents start holding wallets, making payments, and acting independently, knowing that a human exists somewhere behind the agent isn’t the whole problem.

You also need to know who stands behind that specific agent, what it is authorised to do, and who is accountable when it acts.

And all of that needs to happen without publicly exposing the identity underneath.

I think the agent economy is shifting from proof of personhood to proof of accountability.

The signs are everywhere.

I saw that @MetaMask recently published a case study on @GenLayer-powered @courtofinternet.

It mentions an AI-service payment flow they’re still developing. Internet Court’s own write-up uses an example where the dispute is worth just $3.

To give you some more context on this, a traditional smart contract can hold the funds and release them according to fixed rules.

But if there’s an issue like incomplete answers or slower responses than agreed, GenLayer’s Intelligent Contracts can use AI to review the agreed terms and available evidence.

So the flow would look something like this:

→ Both sides agree on requirements upfront, and payment is held in escrow.

→ GenLayer’s Intelligent Contract checks signed service logs against those terms to work out the payout.

→ Independent validators review the evidence and vote on whether the proposed result meets the contract’s criteria. The decision can also be appealed.

Depending on the result, the provider gets paid in full or receives a reduced payout.

This ties back to what I wrote before: agents can already make deals and move money, but they also need a way to settle disagreements when the service doesn’t match what was promised.

That’s the part GenLayer is building for, even when it’s only $3.

What other use cases should I look into?

All cryptographic infrastructure including blockchains has to be rebuilt around this realization. 

That’s it.

my honest answer: 100x is my base case.

they're still at just above 1% of traditional secondary market volume, and the value prop over eBay and Goldin is so obvious that closing that gap is basically just a matter of when anymore.

however, what gets me really excited is that onchain doesn't just move the existing market over, but it has the potential to expand it. better rails mean more collectors and more volume than ever existed before.

tldr: still one of the most asymmetric bets in crypto right now.

Jason Calacanis: Everyday Americans Need to Benefit From the AI Boom

@Jason on the Super Intelligence Summit at the White House:

“Awesome to see the power of all these American industries together.

I think the next piece of this puzzle is to start to include Americans in this, the bottom half of the K-shaped recovery.

Where's the teacher? Where’s the teenager going into college in all of this? Where's the American tool belt worker, the plumber?

It looks from the outside, I think, to a lot of Americans that this is still a bit scary, so there's more work to do there.

I was on a flight on Delta, and the flight attendants asked me what I did, and I was talking to them and they said, ‘I'm so scared of this AI stuff. I'm so glad I'm retiring because I don't want to lose my job.’

Americans are still petrified of this technology. They still think they're losing their jobs. They still think it's dangerous.

So I thought this was a great first step, but there's more work to do to pull Americans back off that ledge.

And we need to, and I think this is where the president or the next president could have a really major impact, is to start forcing American companies to not just think about how they make more money, how they get more green lights for their data centers, how they get less regulation and more free markets, but how does this lower the cost of education? How does this build more homes? How does this help healthcare? How do people get more healthcare at a lower price? None of that was addressed.”

Since we first started measuring economies, GDP has only ever been able to grow three ways. Population growth, plus productivity growth, plus debt growth.

That equation is The Everything Code.

And it's what has left us in the mess we're in today. We have too few workers and too much debt. When productivity cant fill the gap, the only lever left is more debt... and the only way to carry that much debt is to debase the currency. That is why everything feels more expensive every year and why your savings never seem to keep up. 

Except now, for the first time in history, we have a way out.

AI and robots change the equation itself. They add workers that dont age, dont retire, get cheaper every year, and add productivity on a scale we've never seen. 

The catch is that it's now moving faster than society, politics or economics can adapt. Coherence breaks down. That is The Economic Singularity.

This is what my book, The Everything Code, charts. It starts with the framework itself, how debt and demographics got us here, moves through The Exponential Age and ends at The Economic Singularity. Everything Ive been working on for years, in one place and in order, so you can see why we have such a short window to position ourselves before the whole system changes completely.

It's out on November 3rd.

If you're planning to read it, I would be really grateful if you would consider pre-ordering. Pre-orders are what move the rankings, and it would mean a great deal to me.

Thanks!

Feels inevitable to me. If AI keeps getting better at math, it could discover a shortcut for factoring huge numbers, a new attack on elliptic curves, or an entirely different way around the assumptions behind encryption.

Every major lab will race toward this because the advantage would be enormous, both commercially and for national security. You want to be the first to find the weakness and secure your own infrastructure when trillions of dollars flow through it.

Btw, Matthew Green is a cryptography professor at Johns Hopkins.
He also co-created Zerocash, the privacy protocol behind Zcash, so this is very much his field.
